routes.description: Establish the four claimed historical facts from early Christian materials, connect them as a cumulative evidential set, and show that divine resurrection explains that set more adequately than the proposed literary, visionary, or sociological alternatives.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the sources warrant burial, an empty tomb, postmortem appearances, and the disciples’ resurrection belief, and if God raising Jesus provides the best comparative explanation of those facts despite objections from historical analogy and source criticism.

motionBridge.description: Show that the earliest Christian sources establish all four specified facts and that God raising Jesus best explains their conjunction.

centralBridges.description: Establish an identifiable burial and the subsequent discovery of an empty tomb from sufficiently early, independent, and historically credible traditions.
Establish that individuals and groups experienced appearances of Jesus after his death using authentic early testimony and historically usable narrative sources.
Explain why the earliest disciples sincerely adopted a specific resurrection belief despite the crucifixion and the surrounding Jewish expectations.
Demonstrate comparatively that divine resurrection accounts for the combined evidence better than legendary development, cultural borrowing, visions, or belief-preservation mechanisms.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Defend the authenticity, early dating, and historical admissibility of Pauline traditions and the relevant Gospel materials.
Show that proposed pagan and hero-story parallels lack the relevant similarity or causal connection needed to explain the earliest Christian claims.

routes.description: Deny that the surviving sources warrant the four asserted facts or the resurrection inference by applying historical analogy, literary and textual criticism, and ordinary mechanisms for visionary reports, legendary narratives, and the persistence of religious belief.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if material uncertainty remains about one or more foundational facts, or if familiar literary, cultural, visionary, or sociological processes provide sufficient alternatives to prevent divine resurrection from being established as the best historical explanation.

motionBridge.description: Show that the earliest sources do not establish the complete factual conjunction or do not make divine resurrection its best historical explanation.

centralBridges.description: Show that the burial, empty-tomb, and appearance materials are literary, redactional, or textually uncertain enough that the asserted events are not established.
Use comparable ancient vanished-body, apotheosis, dying-and-rising, and appearance narratives to support a legendary or hagiographic account of the traditions.
Provide non-resurrection pathways for exaltation, appearance reports, and continuing faith, including visions, retrojection, syncretism, and cognitive-dissonance reduction.
Show that invoking divine action does not resolve uncertain historical claims or outperform ordinary explanations under a case-by-case evidential method.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Defend historical ideal-type comparison as requiring meaningful structural similarity rather than exact correspondence or direct literary copying.
Limit the evidential reach of Pauline authenticity claims, later disciple traditions, scholarly consensus, and extra-biblical notices.

sections.title: Source Proximity, Textual Integrity, and Historical Method
sections.rationale: The motion depends on whether Pauline and Gospel materials can function as early historical evidence. This section covers their dating, textual integrity, literary character, admissibility, and the role of analogy in evaluating extraordinary ancient claims.

sections.title: Burial Tradition and the Empty Tomb
sections.rationale: A known burial place and the subsequent absence of Jesus’ body form a linked evidential foundation for the bodily-resurrection case, while source criticism and alternative literary explanations contest whether either event is historically established.

sections.title: Nature and Historical Status of the Postmortem Appearances
sections.rationale: The reported experiences of individuals and groups are a principal fact asserted by the motion. Their provenance, visionary or bodily character, and relationship to comparable ancient narratives determine what they can establish historically.

sections.title: Origins of the Disciples’ Resurrection Belief
sections.rationale: The debate must explain why resurrection belief arose and persisted among Jesus’ followers. Jewish expectations and claimed transformation bear on one account, while syncretism, belief development, and cognitive dissonance supply competing mechanisms.

sections.title: Resurrection as the Best Explanation
sections.rationale: Even if some underlying facts are granted, the motion requires a comparative inference to divine resurrection. This section addresses explanatory adequacy, prior probability, the likelihood of the evidence under alternatives, and whether miraculous agency completes that inference.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: Jesus received an honorable burial by Joseph of Arimathea in a known tomb, supported by early Pauline and Markan material and the absence of a rival burial tradition.
moves.attributionBasis: The uninterrupted opening presentation is explicitly introduced as Craig's allotted speech and uses first-person advocacy throughout.

response.rationale: This constructive move directly supplies the burial and identifiable-tomb premise using alleged Pauline and Markan proximity plus the absence of a rival tradition.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it develops a central factual premise with several expressly stated supporting considerations.

precisionFindings.rationale: The burial claim and its sources are recoverable and stable, though the historical confidence appropriate to those sources is only implicitly bounded.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Multiple stated considerations support probability, but early or independent material does not by itself justify the move's comparatively strong historical confidence.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The considerations coherently support burial in a known tomb, with one bounded bridge from source proximity and silence to historical reliability.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Pauline and Markan material and the claimed lack of rivals are specific support, but independence, dating, and argument from silence remain compressed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It occupies the top of the central tier because identifiable burial is an indispensable part of the burial-and-empty-tomb bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move constructs its own burial case and does not meaningfully interpret a developed opposing alternative in this span.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt expressly invokes Mark's very old source, Paul as independent attestation, Joseph of Arimathea, and a known burial tradition.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: Women discovered Jesus' tomb empty on the Sunday after the crucifixion, as supported by Pauline implications, early Markan material, narrative simplicity, and an early hostile explanation presupposing a missing body.
moves.attributionBasis: The same explicitly identified Craig opening speech continues without an intervening speaker change across this complete numbered argument.

response.rationale: This constructive move supplies the empty-tomb half of the central bridge through women discoverers, Pauline implications, Markan material, narrative features, and hostile acknowledgment.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it gives a sustained and multi-part defense of an indispensable factual premise.

precisionFindings.rationale: The claimed event and evidential strands are fully recoverable, with only the degree of historical certainty left as an implicit qualification.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The cumulative considerations plausibly support the claim, but their independence and historical force are asserted more confidently than defended.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The several considerations converge coherently, though the inference from narrative and hostile-response features to factuality retains an implicit bridge.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move offers several concrete source features, but the Pauline implication, Markan antiquity, and hostile tradition require further verification and rival comparison.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The empty tomb is indispensable to the selected central bridge, and this move addresses it directly and extensively.

representationalCharity.rationale: The span primarily builds a positive empty-tomb case rather than evaluating a developed competing interpretation.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt states that women found the tomb empty, links Sunday dating to Paul's information, and locates the narrative in old Markan source material.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: Multiple individuals and groups experienced appearances of Jesus alive after his death, as indicated by Paul's early witness list, his acquaintance with participants, and multiple Gospel strands.
moves.attributionBasis: Craig remains the sole speaker in his announced opening presentation and explicitly introduces this material as his third historical fact.

response.rationale: This constructive move directly advances the appearances bridge by adducing Paul's witness list, participant acquaintance, individual and group experiences, and Gospel strands.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it squarely develops an indispensable appearance premise with multiple stated evidential routes.

precisionFindings.rationale: The proposition is clear, but the term appearances does not consistently distinguish reported experiences, visions, and encounters with a physically present person.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Early testimony supports reported experiences, but near-universal scholarly acknowledgment and the stronger experiential implications exceed what is fully defended here.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Early lists and acquaintance coherently support appearance reports, with an implicit bridge from reports and traditions to the nature of the experiences.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Paul's list and claimed personal links are specific evidence, but source independence, group-report verification, and experiential character remain underdeveloped.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly supplies the central postmortem-appearance premise and therefore sits at the top of its relevance tier.

representationalCharity.rationale: No developed rival account is interpreted in this constructive span, so there is no meaningful charity test to apply.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt explicitly says different individuals and groups saw appearances and cites Paul's quoted eyewitness list and scholarly acknowledgment.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: The original disciples suddenly and sincerely believed Jesus had risen despite a crucified messiah's apparent failure, the stigma of divine curse, and Jewish expectation of a general end-time resurrection.
moves.attributionBasis: The uninterrupted Craig opening identifies this passage as the fourth fact and retains the same first-person argumentative framing.

response.rationale: This constructive move addresses the origin-of-belief bridge by contrasting sincere resurrection belief with crucifixion, curse, messianic disappointment, and Jewish expectations.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it directly develops the central explanatory datum and several contextual reasons that make it surprising.

precisionFindings.rationale: The central claim is recoverable, but generalizations about Jewish messianic and resurrection expectations are broader than the span expressly qualifies.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The contextual tensions support explanatory pressure, but the uniformity of the disciples' predispositions and Jewish expectations is somewhat overstated.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference from contrary expectations to a need for explanation is coherent, though it does not itself identify or prove the resurrection cause.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Several relevant Jewish-context considerations are named, but their breadth, representativeness, and application to all original disciples are compressed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly establishes the surprising origin and sincerity of belief that the central resurrection-belief bridge requires.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move presents contextual obstacles to belief without yet interpreting a sufficiently developed opposing causal account.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt expressly describes sudden sincere belief despite a dead leader and messianic expectations lacking a defeated, crucified messiah.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: God raising Jesus from the dead best explains the burial, empty tomb, appearances, and origin of resurrection belief because the rejected theft and apparent-death theories do not plausibly explain the cumulative facts.
moves.attributionBasis: This is Craig's explicitly signposted second contention near the close of his uninterrupted and formally introduced opening presentation.

response.rationale: This constructive move reaches the motion bridge by combining the asserted facts, rejecting theft and apparent-death theories, and inferring divine resurrection as best explanation.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it directly states the motion-level conclusion, though comparative development is much thinner than the conclusion's importance warrants.

precisionFindings.rationale: The inference and comparison class are recoverable, but the conclusion lacks an explicit condition tying it to the prior establishment of all asserted facts.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Rejecting two old theories and asserting no plausible naturalistic explanation does not supply the full comparative warrant for the strong best-explanation claim.

charity.alternative: Naturalistic explanations may work cumulatively or in combination rather than through the two named older theories.
charity.decisiveQualification: The move expressly discusses theft and apparent death but does not compare the strongest literary, visionary, or sociological alternatives.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The abductive form is usable, but rejection of two alternatives does not complete the inference that divine resurrection best explains the whole set.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move relies heavily on asserted scholarly rejection and absence of alternatives without representative evidence or serious comparison of live rivals.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly states and supports the exact motion-level completion condition, giving it maximal relevance within the motion tier.

representationalCharity.rationale: The naturalistic alternative is narrowed to two rejected theories, omitting decisive contemporary alternatives that the motion-level inference must compare.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt says theft and apparent-death theories are rejected, claims no plausible naturalistic account exists, and names resurrection as the best explanation.

moves.speaker: Robert Price
moves.proposition: Critical historians can assess individual miracle reports without either rejecting every supernatural claim in advance or accepting every reported miracle.
moves.attributionBasis: Price continues his uninterrupted allotted speech, explicitly discusses Craig and apologists, and maintains the same critical argumentative perspective.

components.text: Whether a supernatural explanation may be inferred from the evidence rather than accepted or rejected categorically.

response.rationale: The move contacts the methodological premise behind the best-explanation inference by distinguishing openness to miracles from acceptance of every miracle report, but it does not assess this report's evidence.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: This is a partial answer: it contacts the decisive methodological premise but does not conduct the promised case-specific comparison.

precisionFindings.rationale: The distinction among possibility, general openness, and acceptance of a particular report is explicit and terminologically stable.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The modest logical claim that possibility does not entail actuality is fully warranted and carefully distinguished from metaphysical denial.

charity.alternative: Craig's inference purports to be evidential and case-specific, not a rule accepting every supernatural report.
charity.decisiveQualification: Price correctly preserves case-by-case assessment but does not yet engage Craig's actual comparative evidence.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The modal distinction is explicit and valid: divine capability and miracle possibility do not entail that any particular reported miracle occurred.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The conceptual warrant is strong, but the move supplies no case-specific evidence demonstrating how the distinction resolves the resurrection report.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It materially supports the central explanatory-standard bridge, though it remains methodological rather than a full application to the case.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move fairly avoids charging categorical supernaturalism, though its general principle leaves the strongest case-specific argument unanswered.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt expressly states that belief in God's capability and miracle possibility does not require accepting everything anyone reports.

moves.speaker: Robert Price
moves.proposition: Historical inference depends on analogy between past and present experience, so familiar legendary explanations may be preferred without metaphysically denying miracles.
moves.attributionBasis: The uninterrupted Price speech explicitly introduces the principle of historical analogy and contrasts critical historians with Christian apologists.

components.text: Whether the resurrection inference can outrank familiar explanations despite the historical requirement of analogy with experience.

response.rationale: The move contacts the best-explanation method by arguing that historical inference requires analogy, but its werewolf and fairy-tale illustrations do not compare the specific resurrection evidence.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It is a partial answer that reaches the governing methodological demand while leaving the concrete cumulative evidence substantially untreated.

precisionFindings.rationale: The analogy principle is clear, but its unrestricted formulation risks collapsing graded historical analogy into whatever resembles present ordinary experience.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Some analogical continuity is necessary for inference, but the categorical formulation lacks qualifications for unusual events and differential evidence.

charity.alternative: A resurrection advocate can accept analogical reasoning while claiming unusually strong case-specific evidence for a unique event.
charity.decisiveQualification: The move must show why the evidence fails, not merely compare the claim with werewolves or Jack and the Beanstalk.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The methodological core is coherent, but the examples do not establish that every extraordinary claim has the same evidential status.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move offers vivid analogies but little defended warrant for applying their evidential deficiencies to the specific resurrection materials.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly defends the subsidiary historical-analogy method and therefore sits at the top of that tier.

representationalCharity.rationale: The illustrations materially weaken the strongest evidential version of the opposing position by substituting plainly unsupported fantastic stories.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt states that historical inference assumes analogy with present experience and illustrates the claim with werewolves, alchemy, and a fairy tale.

moves.speaker: Robert Price
moves.proposition: The empty-tomb narrative belongs to a familiar ancient hero-story pattern involving vanished remains, heavenly ascent, appearances, and initial disciple skepticism.
moves.attributionBasis: Price remains the announced speaker and directly contrasts Craig's reading of Mark with ancient biographical parallels cited in his own critique.

components.text: Whether the empty-tomb story's source features warrant history rather than a theological or legendary genre classification.
Whether postmortem appearance narratives share an ancient legendary pattern that reduces their historical force.

response.rationale: The move contacts both empty-tomb historicity and appearance interpretation by locating them within vanished-body hero stories, although the excerpt does not establish detailed structural or causal comparison.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: This partial answer contacts the decisive historical-warrant components for two facts but leaves the proposed genre analogy underdocumented.

precisionFindings.rationale: The genre claim and relevant narrative elements are recoverable, with an implicit rather than explicit limit on what genre resemblance proves.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Ancient parallels can reduce confidence, but the strong genre assignment needs more specific comparative detail than the excerpt supplies.

charity.alternative: The narratives may contain theology while still preserving historically grounded burial, tomb, or appearance information.
charity.decisiveQualification: Genre resemblance alone neither proves literary dependence nor excludes historically transmitted content.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The genre-based defeater is coherent, though similarity must be shown sufficiently and does not alone entail fabrication.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Ancient vanished-body and appearance stories are invoked, but representative parallels and the precise shared structure are not developed in the excerpt.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly advances the central historical-analogy bridge against the empty-tomb and appearance components.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move recognizes Craig's historical reading but treats theological and historical character too nearly as mutually exclusive possibilities.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt calls the empty-tomb story theological and explicitly invokes other ancient vanished-body and postmortem-appearance stories as comparators.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: Greco-Roman hero and dying-god stories do not explain the original disciples' resurrection belief because their categories differ from Jewish resurrection and no plausible causal route to Galilean disciples is shown.
moves.attributionBasis: The speaker change follows applause after Price's speech, and the new speaker directly attacks Price's use of Talbert and defends Craig's previously stated position.

components.text: Whether Greco-Roman parallels supply the right interpretive category and a causal explanation for the disciples' belief.
Whether structural analogy without exact copying is historically relevant even absent a direct causal transmission route.

response.rationale: The reply directly challenges category fit and causal transmission, but it does not answer Price's broader ideal-type claim that analogy can matter without direct literary dependence.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: This partial answer decisively contacts the genre claim's causal and contextual application while leaving the broader analogy method unanswered.

precisionFindings.rationale: The Jewish-context and causal-gap objections are clearly recoverable, though their scope is implicitly limited to explaining the earliest disciples.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Category and causal differences are material, but declaring pagan mythology simply wrong exceeds the limited comparison supplied here.

charity.alternative: Ancient parallels can function as ideal-type comparisons without direct copying or a single traceable causal chain.
charity.decisiveQualification: A causal gap defeats borrowing claims more readily than it defeats broader genre or cultural-analogy arguments.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Different categories and absent causal transmission coherently weaken a borrowing explanation, with a bounded gap regarding noncausal analogy.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The Jewish interpretive context is specifically asserted, but the historical insulation from Greco-Roman culture and detailed category comparison remain compressed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It attacks the central historical-analogy bridge directly, especially its capacity to explain the origin of belief.

representationalCharity.rationale: The response fairly raises contextual dissimilarity but construes the analogy too narrowly as requiring direct causal transmission.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt says Greco-Roman biography is the wrong interpretive context, identifies a Jewish context, and denies a causal connection to disciples' belief.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: First Corinthians 15:3–11 is authentic rather than interpolated because all manuscripts contain it, early writers cite it, its vocabulary and pronouns fit the context, and its removal damages Paul's argument.
moves.attributionBasis: Craig identifies Price’s interpolation theory by name and develops a continuous external-and-internal-evidence rebuttal in his own speaking turn.

components.text: Whether the Pauline appearance material should be assessed through concrete textual evidence rather than general methodological reservations.
Whether analogy defeats the authenticity and historical usability of First Corinthians 15.

response.rationale: The legal earlier targets do not contain Price's interpolation theory itself; the reply supplies issue-bearing textual evidence but does not contact their decisive methodological demands.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It is a relevant nonanswer to the exposed targets: valuable source criticism that does not answer their central method claims.

precisionFindings.rationale: The authenticity claim, passage boundaries, and external and internal evidential categories are clearly and consistently specified.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The convergence of manuscript, patristic, vocabulary, pronoun, and contextual considerations fits a strong but non-certain authenticity conclusion.

charity.alternative: The passage may be a composite or interpolated creed despite universal manuscript attestation.
charity.decisiveQualification: A late interpolation would need to precede all surviving manuscripts and early citations while also explaining the contextual fit.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Several independent authenticity indicators converge explicitly, and the response addresses alleged contradiction and contextual disruption.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move supplies representative external and internal textual considerations, with only detailed documentation of manuscripts and citations compressed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the central source-historicity challenge to a principal early appearance text.

representationalCharity.rationale: The response addresses both external and internal versions of the interpolation theory and identifies concrete difficulties without reducing it to mere skepticism.

moves.evidenceBasis: The span invokes universal manuscript inclusion, early citations, vocabulary and pronoun continuity, Galatians context, and damage caused by removing the passage.

moves.speaker: Robert Price
moves.proposition: First Corinthians 15:3–11 is plausibly a later composite creed whose tensions and institutional features weaken its value as early evidence for resurrection appearances.
moves.attributionBasis: The post-applause speaker directly states his interpolation theory and answers Craig’s specific textual, historical, and contextual objections.

components.text: Whether First Corinthians 15:3–11 is authentic and early enough to warrant the claimed appearance evidence.
Whether Paul's witness list guarantees historically early individual and group appearance testimony.

response.rationale: The reply directly contests authenticity and evidential proximity through form-critical, composite, institutional, and contextual considerations, though it does not fully rebut every manuscript and citation point.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: This is a strong partial answer contacting the decisive authenticity and appearance-evidence demands while leaving some external evidence untreated.

precisionFindings.rationale: The move consistently presents interpolation as likely rather than certain and identifies the specific passage and textual features at issue.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The form-critical observations make interpolation possible, but creed form and compositeness do not strongly date insertion without further evidence.

charity.alternative: Early creed form and universal textual attestation can support authenticity rather than lateness.
charity.decisiveQualification: A composite traditional formula can be early and authentically quoted by Paul even if Paul did not compose every phrase.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Textual tensions can support interpolation, but the inference from creed form and institutional features to later insertion retains substantial unsupported conditionals.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Several textual features are identified, yet dating them as late and overcoming universal attestation require documentation and comparative textual evidence not supplied.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central source-historicity bridge by challenging the principal early appearance passage.

representationalCharity.rationale: The response engages Craig's contextual points but gives insufficient weight to the strongest distinction between Pauline quotation and later interpolation.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt calls the passage a creed and composite digest of formulaic fragments and associates creed form with a later institutional setting.

moves.speaker: Robert Price
moves.proposition: Resurrection belief could have arisen by retrojecting an expected future return of Jesus into the past as prior appearances, leaving multiple historical possibilities open.
moves.attributionBasis: Price continues his closing statement, proposing a developmental reconstruction of early belief and drawing an explicit methodological conclusion about historical uncertainty.

components.text: What non-resurrection developmental pathway could produce the disciples' resurrection and appearance beliefs.
Whether a non-pagan, internal developmental mechanism can explain the belief without a borrowing route.

response.rationale: The move supplies an internal developmental alternative—retrojection of expected return into prior appearances—and expressly frames it as a possibility rather than a demonstrated history.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: This partial answer contacts the decisive causal demand but offers only a possible pathway, not a comparably evidenced reconstruction.

precisionFindings.rationale: Retrojection, its proposed temporal direction, and the limited claim of possibility are all recoverable and explicitly qualified.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Price repeatedly says he does not know whether this occurred and uses the reconstruction only to establish multiple historical possibilities.

charity.alternative: The earliest disciples' belief may have followed experiences they interpreted as appearances rather than later retrojection.
charity.decisiveQualification: Showing a conceivable development does not establish that it occurred or explain the earliest timing and distribution of reports.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The developmental pathway is internally coherent and modestly framed, though several historical transitions remain implicit.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move offers a plausible reconstruction and one saying tradition, but lacks representative evidence dating the stages or demonstrating retrojection.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central belief-alternatives bridge by proposing a non-resurrection origin for appearance traditions.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move does not claim to disprove the opposing history and explicitly preserves uncertainty, although its alternative remains weakly evidenced.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt proposes that an expected return and resurrection were retrojected into the past, while expressly stating that the speaker does not know what happened.

moves.speaker: Robert Price
moves.proposition: Even if a resurrection is conceivable, extant narratives characterized as literary creations do not provide adequate historical evidence for confidence that it occurred.
moves.attributionBasis: Price directly answers the respondent's consistency challenge and carefully distinguishes metaphysical possibility from what the surviving texts historically warrant.

components.text: Whether the surviving narratives establish the factual conjunction strongly enough to support the resurrection inference.
Whether authentic textual transmission alone establishes the historical truth of the narrated or reported events.

response.rationale: The move directly distinguishes metaphysical possibility from historical warrant and denies that the available literary texts establish the facts, though its source critique remains generalized.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the decisive motion-level evidential demand but only partly answers because the individual source arguments are not analyzed here.

precisionFindings.rationale: The possibility-warrant distinction is clear, but describing the texts collectively as literary rather than historical leaves the categories somewhat overbroad.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The explicit concession that Craig could be right is well calibrated, although wholesale evidential insufficiency is asserted with limited source-specific defense.

charity.alternative: Literary and theological narratives can still contain historically usable testimony and source traditions.
charity.decisiveQualification: Literary construction limits evidential weight but does not automatically erase all historical value.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The distinction between conceivable occurrence and inadequate evidence is valid, with a material ambiguity in the literary-versus-historical classification.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move asserts narrative credulity and literary creation but supplies little representative analysis of the texts needed for the broad conclusion.

relevanceBurden.rationale: By denying that the sources establish the factual conjunction, it directly supplies the con motion-level completion condition.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move fairly concedes possible truth but treats literary character too readily as sufficient for broad historical inadmissibility.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt explicitly concedes that resurrection could have occurred while denying that the extant texts provide adequate historical evidence.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: New Testament writings should be evaluated as separate first-century historical documents rather than collectively disqualified because the church later assembled them into a canon.
moves.attributionBasis: The question is explicitly addressed to Craig, and the sustained first-person answer restates the method used in his presentation.

components.text: Whether later canonical collection disqualifies the component first-century documents from ordinary historical evaluation.
Whether source criticism must evaluate individual passages rather than dismissing the canonical collection as a unit.

response.rationale: The reply correctly reframes the canon as separate documents for assessment and contacts one possible basis for exclusion, but it does not answer Price's literary and redactional objections to those documents.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: This is a partial answer contacting document admissibility while leaving the decisive source-quality criticism substantially unanswered.

precisionFindings.rationale: The methodological claim about separate documents is clear, with only an implicit qualification that admissibility does not establish reliability.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Separate evaluation is warranted, but the assertion that canonical selection captured the earliest and closest sources needs independent support.

charity.alternative: Price's objection concerns literary and historical quality, not mere inclusion in a later canon.
charity.decisiveQualification: Separate-document admissibility does not answer redactional, legendary, or source-dependence concerns.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Later collection does not logically erase the documents' individual provenance, though canonical inclusion itself does not confer reliability.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: First-century document types are specifically identified, but the historical claim about selection for apostolic proximity is asserted rather than defended.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the central source-historicity bridge's broad exclusion of the documents, but not its detailed criticisms.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move offers a sound methodological correction but only partially represents the strongest version of the source-quality objection.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt identifies letters, Gospels, and Acts as separate Greek first-century documents later assembled into a single canonical cover.

moves.speaker: Robert Price
moves.proposition: The burial and empty-tomb accounts are not established facts because their narrative sources are historically problematic and alternative literary explanations remain available.
moves.attributionBasis: Price explicitly turns to points he was accused of neglecting and sequentially addresses Joseph’s burial and the empty tomb.

components.text: Whether the narrative source quality warrants belief in Joseph's burial of Jesus.
Whether the same source-quality and literary-alternative problems prevent establishing the empty tomb.
Whether treating canonical writings separately establishes their historical reliability.

response.rationale: The reply directly challenges burial and empty-tomb warrant by separating mere possibility from justified belief and citing narrative problems, though it gives few concrete examples.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts all principal factual and source-admissibility demands, but the decisive source defects are described rather than demonstrated.

precisionFindings.rationale: The conclusion and possibility concession are clear, but the transcript's apparent 'marbles' wording and broad historical-problems category reduce terminological precision.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move carefully concedes Joseph could have buried Jesus, but low confidence in both accounts rests on largely unspecified source defects.

charity.alternative: Early traditions within a problematic narrative can still preserve a historical burial and empty-tomb report.
charity.decisiveQualification: General narrative difficulties do not automatically defeat the specific traditions without showing relevance to them.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Poor source quality can lower confidence, but the move needs a clearer bridge from general narrative problems to these particular episodes.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Historical difficulties, anachronisms, and literary alternatives are mentioned only generally, without representative examples tied to burial or tomb.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central source-historicity bridge against both burial and empty-tomb foundations.

representationalCharity.rationale: The response acknowledges factual possibility but gives insufficient attention to the opponent's specific early-source and attestation arguments.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt distinguishes possible burial from warranted burial and cites narrative marvels, historical difficulties, anachronisms, and source quality.

moves.speaker: Robert Price
moves.proposition: Gospel appearance accounts have limited historical value because visions of Jesus are common and the narratives contain redactional and legendary material.
moves.attributionBasis: Price introduces appearances as the next disputed fact and states his assessment of the relevant Gospel evidence directly.

components.text: Whether the Gospel texts provide reliable evidence that individuals and groups experienced postmortem appearances.
Whether individual admissibility of Gospel documents establishes substantial historical value for their appearance narratives.

response.rationale: The reply contacts the appearance-evidence demand through vision frequency and alleged redactional and legendary deposits, but it does not address Paul's early witness list.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: This partial answer directly contacts Gospel evidential value while leaving the earlier Pauline component of the appearance case unanswered.

precisionFindings.rationale: The low-value conclusion is recoverable, but 'visions,' appearances, and seeing the risen Jesus are not clearly differentiated.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The speaker repeatedly allows that appearances may have occurred, but the low evidential verdict rests on underdeveloped redactional assertions.

charity.alternative: The appearance case also rests on Paul's earlier testimony and may preserve experiences beneath later Gospel redaction.
charity.decisiveQualification: Legendary development in Gospel narratives does not eliminate the evidential value of every underlying report.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Redaction and common visionary experiences can limit what narratives prove, but neither consideration alone defeats all underlying appearance testimony.

moves.speaker: Robert Price
moves.proposition: The Jesus movement's continuation can be explained through cognitive-dissonance reduction and reinterpretation of disconfirmation without positing a resurrection experience.
moves.attributionBasis: Price explicitly turns to what transformed the disciples and develops the answer through several comparative religious movements.

components.text: How a defeated messianic movement could persist and reinterpret disconfirmation without a resurrection event.
Whether ordinary belief-preservation mechanisms provide a rival explanation for continuing faith.

response.rationale: The move directly supplies cognitive-dissonance reduction as a mechanism and uses comparative movements to show persistence after disconfirmation, while not fully explaining appearance reports.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: This partial answer strongly contacts belief persistence and reinterpretation but does not account for every component of the cumulative evidence.

precisionFindings.rationale: The psychological mechanism and limited target of movement persistence are clear, though applicability to the earliest disciples is implicitly rather than explicitly qualified.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Comparative persistence examples reasonably support a probable available mechanism, provided the claim is limited to continuation and reinterpretation.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Several comparative religious examples support the general mechanism, though their similarity to the earliest Jesus movement is not fully defended.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly advances the central belief-alternatives bridge by explaining persistence after crucifixion and apparent disconfirmation.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move squarely addresses movement survival but only partly engages the stronger demand concerning the specific form of resurrection belief.

moves.speaker: Robert Price
moves.proposition: Invoking a miracle does not explain uncertain historical events because it replaces the disputed event with an even less understood causal claim.
moves.attributionBasis: This is Price’s concluding argumentative point before yielding the floor, expressed through an explicit analogy to a purported explanation.

components.text: Whether naming miraculous agency genuinely explains the disputed historical facts better than rival accounts.
Whether document admissibility resolves the underlying uncertainty that the miracle inference is meant to explain.

response.rationale: The reply contacts the decisive explanatory-adequacy demand by arguing that a miracle label adds an even less understood cause, but it does not compare predictive fit or specific evidence.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: This partial answer reaches the central explanatory inference while leaving the likelihood and comparative-evidence dimensions untreated.

precisionFindings.rationale: The explanatory objection is clear, although it implicitly targets bare miracle invocation rather than every developed theistic causal hypothesis.

calibrationFindings.rationale: A bare miracle label can be explanatorily thin, but the UFO analogy overstates parity with a hypothesis embedded in a broader theistic argument.

charity.alternative: A divine-resurrection hypothesis may predict the evidence under a broader theistic context rather than merely label ignorance.
charity.decisiveQualification: Explanatory unfamiliarity alone does not show that a hypothesis lacks likelihood, scope, or comparative power.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The regress-like objection to unexplained agency is intelligible, but less understood causes can still explain if they entail or predict evidence.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move relies almost entirely on analogy and does not examine the resurrection hypothesis's stated explanatory scope or likelihood.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central explanatory-standard bridge against the motion's culminating best-explanation inference.

representationalCharity.rationale: The UFO analogy substantially weakens the strongest opposing account by treating it as an unsupported appeal to an arbitrary unknown cause.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt says miracle invocation explains an unknown by something still less understood and compares it to attributing pyramid construction to UFOs.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: Assessing resurrection requires considering not only prior improbability but also how unlikely the empty tomb, appearances, and disciples' faith would be if no resurrection occurred.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator directs the question to Craig, and the ensuing uninterrupted first-person response explicitly develops his established resurrection argument.

components.text: The objection wrongly treats prior improbability or causal unfamiliarity as sufficient without considering the likelihood of the evidence if no resurrection occurred.
Whether the empty tomb, appearances, and faith are sufficiently established to enter the likelihood comparison.
Whether cognitive dissonance makes the full conjunction of tomb, appearances, and faith likely without resurrection.

response.rationale: The response expressly diagnoses a missing likelihood term and states its consequence for comparative assessment, but it assumes rather than re-establishes the disputed evidential facts.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It provides an explicit diagnostic defeat of the explanatory objection while only partially answering source-warrant and alternative-mechanism components.
